> This standard establishes the Gainwell Enterprise User Roles Architecture — a reusable, governance-centered role model that defines enterprise role archetypes, product extension rules, role lifecycle governance, and separation-of-duties constraints. All Gainwell products, delivery organizations, and DDI implementations SHALL adopt this standard as the foundation for role engineering.

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#10-executive-summary]

## 1.0 Executive Summary

Gainwell Technologies operates a broad portfolio of healthcare and human services software products deployed across dozens of state programs, Medicaid Management Information System (MMIS) implementations, and delivery partner engagements. Each product has historically defined its own access model, resulting in inconsistent role naming, duplicate engineering effort, divergent onboarding processes, and increasing audit exposure.

This standard establishes the **Gainwell Enterprise User Roles Architecture (GEURA)** — a governance-centered, business-facing role taxonomy that all products, delivery organizations, and Design, Development, and Implementation (DDI) partners SHALL use as the foundation for role engineering.

GEURA does not prescribe entitlement bundles, replace existing product permission models, or mandate a specific IAM platform. It establishes five **Enterprise Role Archetypes** as reusable business abstractions, defines a four-tier **Product Extension Model** for layering product-specific personas and state-specific roles on top of those archetypes, and specifies the governance rules that keep the taxonomy coherent over time.

Adoption of this standard reduces role proliferation, creates a shared language for access review, and positions Gainwell for future identity governance automation without requiring a transformation program today.

---

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#20-problem-statement]

## 2.0 Problem Statement

Gainwell's current access management landscape is product-fragmented. Each product team independently defines roles at the time of implementation, driven by the requirements of individual state contracts rather than by an enterprise model. This pattern produces the following systemic problems:

**Role Inconsistency** — Role names and purposes vary across products. A "Provider Manager" in one product may carry materially different responsibilities than a "Provider Manager" in another. There is no shared vocabulary.

**Duplicate Engineering** — Every new product or DDI engagement begins role engineering from scratch. The same conceptual roles are re-derived repeatedly, consuming design effort that could be directed elsewhere.

**Divergent Onboarding** — Provisioning processes differ across products. State program administrators and Gainwell operations staff must learn different role structures for each system they support.

**Audit and Compliance Exposure** — Access reviews and HIPAA-related audits require demonstrating that user access is appropriate and consistently governed. Without a common role model, demonstrating enterprise-level governance consistency is difficult.

**Scalability Constraints** — As Gainwell pursues identity governance initiatives, automation of access review and role certification is impeded by the absence of a common role taxonomy.

This standard directly addresses these problems by establishing a shared enterprise foundation that products build upon rather than reinvent.

---

## 3.0 Business Drivers

| Driver | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Audit Readiness** | Access reviews under HIPAA, CMS oversight, and state contractual requirements demand demonstrable consistency in how user access is defined and governed across programs. |
| **Operational Efficiency** | A shared role vocabulary reduces onboarding time for operations staff supporting multiple products and state deployments. |
| **DDI Consistency** | DDI partners require clear guidance on how to define roles for state programs. An enterprise model reduces the variation introduced at delivery time. |
| **Identity Governance Readiness** | Future investments in Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) tooling require a clean, structured role taxonomy as a prerequisite. This standard creates that foundation. |
| **Risk Reduction** | Inconsistent role definitions create over-provisioning risk. A governed enterprise model establishes the baseline needed to identify and remediate excess access over time. |
| **Scalability** | As Gainwell expands its product portfolio, a reusable role foundation prevents technical debt accumulation in identity and access management. |

---

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#40-scope]

## 4.0 Scope

This standard applies to:

- All Gainwell-owned and Gainwell-operated software products
- All products integrated into Gainwell platform services
- All DDI engagements where Gainwell defines the reference role model for a state deployment
- All new product development and implementation efforts commencing after the effective date of this standard
- All existing products undergoing access model redesign, significant role restructuring, or IGA integration work

This standard governs:

- Enterprise Role Archetype definitions and their authoritative ownership
- The Product Extension Model and the rules for extending archetypes into product-specific personas
- Role naming conventions within the enterprise taxonomy
- Governance processes for creating, modifying, and retiring enterprise roles and product personas
- Role lifecycle management obligations
- Separation of duties constraints applicable at the enterprise archetype level

---

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#50-out-of-scope]

## 5.0 Out of Scope

The following are explicitly outside the scope of this standard. They may be referenced as future directions but SHALL NOT be treated as requirements of this standard:

| Out-of-Scope Item | Rationale |
|-------------------|-----------|
| **Entitlement rationalization** | Mapping enterprise roles to fine-grained permissions within existing products is a product-level responsibility, not an enterprise governance function at this time. |
| **Authorization modernization** | Migration to Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC), or externalized policy decision engines is a future architectural initiative. |
| **IGA platform selection or implementation** | This standard does not select, recommend, or require any specific Identity Governance and Administration product. |
| **Zero Trust authorization architecture** | Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) and Policy Decision Point (PDP) patterns are future-state. |
| **Enterprise entitlement catalogs** | Centralized, machine-readable entitlement inventories are a future IGA deliverable. |
| **Existing product permission models** | Application-level permissions and entitlements remain product-owned and are not restructured by this standard. |
| **State-specific contractual role requirements** | This standard provides a foundation that state programs extend. It does not supersede contractual obligations for specific role definitions. |

---

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#60-architecture-principles]

## 6.0 Architecture Principles

The following principles govern the design and application of the Gainwell Enterprise User Roles Architecture. These principles take precedence in the event of conflicting guidance from product or program-level decisions.

| ID | Principle | Statement |
|----|-----------|-----------|
| **P-01** | **Enterprise-First Role Foundation** | Every product SHALL derive its role model from Gainwell-defined enterprise role archetypes. Products SHALL NOT create enterprise-level role taxonomies independently. |
| **P-02** | **Layered Extension** | Products MAY extend enterprise archetypes with product-specific business personas. States and DDIs MAY extend product personas with state-specific roles. Neither extension SHALL redefine an enterprise archetype. |
| **P-03** | **Business-Facing Abstractions** | Enterprise role archetypes are business-facing abstractions, not permission bundles. An archetype describes a category of user responsibility; it does not specify what actions that user may take in any given system. |
| **P-04** | **Product Entitlement Sovereignty** | Existing application permissions, entitlements, and authorization logic remain product-owned. This standard governs the role taxonomy above the entitlement layer. |
| **P-05** | **Governance Before Entitlement Standardization** | Role taxonomy governance is the immediate priority. Entitlement rationalization is a subsequent, product-driven activity. |
| **P-06** | **Automation Readiness Without Automation Dependency** | The role model SHALL be designed to support future provisioning automation, access certification, and identity governance without requiring those capabilities to be present today. |
| **P-07** | **Security Architecture as Governance, Not Owner** | Security Architecture provides governance guidance and quality oversight for the role model. Security Architecture does not own business roles. Product business owners are accountable for role purpose and role assignment criteria. |
| **P-08** | **Business Owner Accountability** | Product business owners SHALL remain accountable for defining role purpose, role assignment criteria, and role review decisions. Role design is a business function, not an IT function. |
| **P-09** | **Minimum Disruption Adoption** | Adoption of this standard SHALL be implementable incrementally, with minimum disruption to existing authorization models and without requiring a dedicated transformation program. |
| **P-10** | **Role Model Stability** | Enterprise role archetypes SHALL be changed infrequently and only through formal Enterprise Architecture governance. Stability of the enterprise layer is essential to the integrity of product and state extensions built upon it. |

---

### Tier Definitions

| Tier | Name | Governed By | Approved By | Description |
|------|------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| 1 | Enterprise Archetype | Enterprise Architecture | EA Review Board | Stable, business-facing role categories applicable across all products. Defines the type of user, not the actions they perform. |
| 2 | Business Persona | Product Business Owner | Product Owner + EA approval for new archetypes | Product-specific expressions of an enterprise archetype. Describes the role a user plays within a specific product domain. |
| 3 | Product Role | Product Engineering | Product Engineering | Technical implementation of a business persona within a product's authorization system. |
| 4 | Product Entitlements | Product Engineering | Product Engineering | The fine-grained permissions, scopes, or claims assigned to a product role. Product-owned and not governed by this standard. |

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#80-enterprise-role-archetypes]

## 8.0 Enterprise Role Archetypes

The following five archetypes form the Tier 1 enterprise role taxonomy. All products SHALL map their business personas to at least one of these archetypes. New archetypes MAY be proposed through the governance process defined in Section 11.0, but SHALL NOT be created unilaterally by products.

This model is capability-based rather than organizational-hierarchy-based. Products SHALL distinguish roles by access intent and authority (operational, elevated operational, business administration, and security administration), not by job title progression (e.g., Supervisor → Manager → Director).

---
page_texts.13:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#81-viewer]

### 8.1 Viewer

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Archetype ID** | `ENT-ROLE-001` |
| **Archetype Name** | Viewer |
| **Access Posture** | Read-only access to product data and functionality. No ability to create, modify, approve, or administer. |

**Purpose**
The Viewer archetype represents users whose access is limited to observing system data. Users in this archetype consume information but do not participate in operational workflows, approvals, or administrative functions.

**Typical Responsibilities**
- Review records, reports, and dashboards for informational purposes
- Monitor status of transactions, claims, or enrollments
- Export or retrieve data under defined business rules
- Support audit, oversight, or reporting functions

**Example Product Personas**

| Product | Business Persona |
|---------|-----------------|
| Pharmacy | Read-Only User |
| Provider+ | Provider Roster Reviewer |
| CEF | Eligibility Inquiry Analyst |
| MMIS | Program Monitor |

**Governance Notes**
- Products SHALL NOT assign write or approval entitlements to roles mapped to this archetype.
- Where a user requires both read and limited write access, a separate persona mapped to Operational User is appropriate.

---
page_texts.14:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#82-operational-user]

### 8.2 Operational User

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Archetype ID** | `ENT-ROLE-002` |
| **Archetype Name** | Operational User |
| **Access Posture** | Day-to-day business processing access within defined product scope. No broad administrative authority. |

**Purpose**
The Operational User archetype represents the primary workforce personas who perform core business processing activities in a product.

**Typical Responsibilities**
- Process transactions, claims, prior authorizations, and enrollment actions
- Enter, update, and submit operational data within assigned scope
- Execute standard workflows following established business rules
- Escalate exceptions to elevated operational personnel

**Example Product Personas**

| Product | Business Persona |
|---------|-----------------|
| Pharmacy | Claims Processor |
| Provider+ | Provider Enrollment Specialist |
| CEF | Eligibility Verification Worker |
| MMIS | Case Worker |

**Governance Notes**
- Personas derived from this archetype SHALL be scoped to a defined functional domain within the product.
- Separation of duties rules (Section 13.0) SHALL be applied when assigning this archetype alongside elevated operational or administrative archetypes.

---
page_texts.15:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#83-elevated-operational-user]

### 8.3 Elevated Operational User

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Archetype ID** | `ENT-ROLE-003` |
| **Archetype Name** | Elevated Operational User |
| **Access Posture** | Operational access plus elevated business workflow authority such as approval, escalation, override, or specialized review authority. |

**Purpose**
The Elevated Operational User archetype represents users who perform specialized or elevated business functions beyond standard operational processing. This includes approval authority, review authority, and workflow override authority regardless of organizational title.

**Typical Responsibilities**
- All responsibilities of Operational User within the same domain
- Approve, reject, or return work items submitted by team members
- Perform workflow overrides within defined thresholds
- Conduct specialized review functions (e.g., clinical review, escalations)
- Provide leadership functions within business operations

**Example Product Personas**

| Product | Business Persona |
|---------|-----------------|
| Pharmacy | Claims Supervisor, Clinical Pharmacist, Medical Director |
| Provider+ | Enrollment Supervisor |
| CEF | Eligibility Team Lead |
| MMIS | Unit Supervisor |

**Governance Notes**
- This archetype replaces enterprise-level Supervisor and Manager separation with a capability-based elevated operations construct.
- Products SHALL document the approval thresholds and override limits applicable to each elevated persona.
- Products SHALL enforce maker-checker controls that prevent users from approving or overriding their own submissions in the same domain.

---
page_texts.16:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#84-business-administrator]

### 8.4 Business Administrator

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Archetype ID** | `ENT-ROLE-004` |
| **Archetype Name** | Business Administrator |
| **Access Posture** | Administration of application business configuration, reference data, workflow settings, and operational parameters. Not intended for security administration. |

**Purpose**
The Business Administrator archetype represents personas with authority to configure application behavior and operational settings required for business execution.

**Typical Responsibilities**
- Configure business rules, thresholds, and workflow parameters
- Manage reference data and operational settings
- Administer product configuration needed for business operations
- Support business-facing troubleshooting and configuration audits

**Example Product Personas**

| Product | Business Persona |
|---------|-----------------|
| Pharmacy | Pharmacy Configuration Admin |
| Provider+ | Provider+ Application Admin |
| CEF | CEF Configuration Admin |
| State | State Program Administrator |

**Governance Notes**
- Business Administrator assignments SHALL require documented business justification and at least annual review.
- Business Administrators SHALL NOT concurrently hold Security Administrator assignments in the same product.
- For production systems, products SHOULD implement time-bounded or just-in-time (JIT) workflows for this archetype, consistent with [GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06](../../../strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06.md).

---
page_texts.17:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#85-security-administrator]

### 8.5 Security Administrator

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Archetype ID** | `ENT-ROLE-005` |
| **Archetype Name** | Security Administrator |
| **Access Posture** | Security policy enforcement, audit access, and security configuration authority within the product. Elevated privilege requiring enhanced governance controls. |

**Purpose**
The Security Administrator archetype represents security-privileged personas with authority to manage security configuration, review audit logs, manage elevated access, and enforce security policy at the product level.

**Typical Responsibilities**
- Manage product security configuration including authentication policies, session parameters, and IP restrictions
- Access security and audit logs for investigation or compliance review
- Approve or reject requests for elevated access within the product
- Conduct access reviews and certify role assignments
- Coordinate with enterprise IAM and Security Architecture on security incidents

**Example Product Personas**

| Product | Business Persona |
|---------|-----------------|
| Pharmacy | Pharmacy Security Officer |
| Provider+ | Provider+ Security Admin |
| CEF | CEF Compliance Administrator |
| Enterprise | IAM Platform Administrator |

**Governance Notes**
- Security Administrator assignments SHALL require approval by both the Product Security Owner and Security Architecture.
- Security Administrators SHALL NOT concurrently hold Business Administrator assignments in the same product.
- Activity performed under this archetype SHALL generate audit log entries retained per Gainwell retention standards.
- Products SHOULD implement time-bounded or just-in-time (JIT) provisioning for Security Administrator personas.

---

## 9.0 Product Extension Model

Products extend the enterprise archetype taxonomy by defining **Business Personas** (Tier 2) that map to one or more enterprise archetypes. Products SHALL NOT bypass Tier 1 or introduce role concepts that exist outside the archetype taxonomy without formal EA approval.
page_texts.19:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#91-extension-rules]

### 9.1 Extension Rules

| Rule ID | Rule | Normative Level |
|---------|------|-----------------|
| **EXT-01** | Every Business Persona SHALL be mapped to exactly one primary Enterprise Role Archetype. | SHALL |
| **EXT-02** | A Business Persona MAY reference a secondary archetype where its responsibilities span two archetype categories, subject to separation of duties review. | MAY |
| **EXT-03** | Business Personas SHALL NOT expand the access posture of their mapped archetype. A persona mapped to Viewer SHALL NOT grant write access. | SHALL |
| **EXT-04** | Business Persona names SHALL be meaningful to business stakeholders, not technical in nature. Names SHALL use business domain vocabulary, not system or technical terminology. | SHALL |
| **EXT-05** | State-specific role extensions SHALL be documented in a state role extension register maintained by the DDI. State extensions extend Tier 3 product roles, not Tier 2 business personas. The register SHALL be available to Gainwell Enterprise Architecture upon request. | SHALL |
| **EXT-06** | Products SHALL maintain a Role-to-Archetype mapping register, updated whenever personas are added or modified. | SHALL |
| **EXT-07** | DDIs MAY create state-specific role extensions that further restrict (not expand) the entitlement scope of a Tier 3 product role for a particular state deployment. | MAY |
page_texts.20:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#92-persona-naming-convention]

### 9.2 Persona Naming Convention

Business Personas SHALL follow the naming pattern:

```
[Product Domain] + [Functional Qualifier] + [Archetype-Aligned Term]
```

| Archetype | Archetype-Aligned Term Examples |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| Viewer | Auditor, Reviewer, Monitor, Analyst |
| Operational User | Specialist, Worker, Processor, Coordinator |
| Elevated Operational User | Supervisor, Lead, Clinical Reviewer, Approver |
| Business Administrator | Administrator, Admin, Configuration Admin |
| Security Administrator | Security Officer, Security Admin, Compliance Admin |

#### New Enterprise Role Archetype

A new Tier 1 Enterprise Role Archetype is a high-governance event. Enterprise archetypes SHALL be added only when a new category of user responsibility cannot be adequately expressed by an extension of an existing archetype.

| Step | Action | Responsible |
|------|--------|-------------|
| 1 | Submit proposal to EA Review Board with business justification and evidence that no existing archetype is sufficient | Proposing product or program |
| 2 | Review by Security Architecture for SoD implications | Security Architecture |
| 3 | Approval by EA Review Board | Enterprise Architecture |
| 4 | Update this standard and notify all affected products | Enterprise Architecture |

### 11.3 Governance Cadence

| Activity | Frequency | Owner |

## 12.0 Role Lifecycle Management

Enterprise role archetypes and product business personas pass through defined lifecycle states. Lifecycle management ensures that the role model remains accurate, auditable, and reflective of current business need.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Proposed : Stakeholder requests new role
    Proposed --> UnderReview : Submitted for governance review
    UnderReview --> Approved : Governance approval received
    UnderReview --> Rejected : Not approved — archived with rationale
    Approved --> Active : Role published and available for assignment
    Active --> UnderReview : Change requested
    Active --> Deprecated : Superseded or no longer needed
    Deprecated --> Retired : All assignments removed; archived
    Retired --> [*]
```
page_texts.31:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#lifecycle-state-definitions]

### Lifecycle State Definitions

| State | Description | Allowed Transitions |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| **Proposed** | Role has been requested but not yet formally reviewed | → Under Review |
| **Under Review** | Role is in governance review | → Approved, → Rejected |
| **Approved** | Role has passed governance review and is cleared for publication | → Active |
| **Rejected** | Role was not approved; rationale documented | Terminal (archived) |
| **Active** | Role is published and available for assignment | → Under Review (for changes), → Deprecated |
| **Deprecated** | Role is no longer recommended for new assignments; existing assignments may remain during wind-down | → Retired |
| **Retired** | All assignments removed; role archived | Terminal |
page_texts.32:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#lifecycle-obligations]

### Lifecycle Obligations

- Products SHALL NOT assign users to Deprecated roles after the deprecation effective date without documented exception.
- Enterprise Architecture SHALL notify all affected products at least 90 days before retiring an enterprise archetype.
- Products SHALL remove all assignments to a retired archetype mapping within 180 days of retirement notice.
- Rejected role proposals SHALL be retained with documented rationale for a minimum of three years.
- Products SHOULD periodically deactivate inactive Security Administrator assignments. An assignment with no recorded activity for 90 days SHOULD be reviewed for deactivation or time-bound renewal, consistent with [GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06](../../../strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06.md).

## 13.0 Separation of Duties Considerations

Separation of Duties (SoD) prevents conflict of interest and reduces fraud risk by ensuring that no individual holds roles whose combined authority would allow them to execute and approve their own actions, or to administer their own access.
page_texts.34:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#131-enterprise-level-sod-constraints]

### 13.1 Enterprise-Level SoD Constraints

The following SoD constraints apply at the archetype level across all products. Products SHALL enforce these constraints and MAY define additional product-specific SoD rules.

| Constraint ID | Archetype A | Archetype B | Constraint Type | Notes |
|---------------|-------------|-------------|-----------------|-------|
| **SOD-01** | Operational User | Elevated Operational User (same domain) | Hard Conflict — SHALL NOT | A user who processes work SHALL NOT also approve or override their own work in the same functional domain. |
| **SOD-02** | Business Administrator | Security Administrator (same product) | Hard Conflict — SHALL NOT | Business administration and security administration authority in the same product SHALL NOT be held concurrently. |
| **SOD-03** | Operational User | Business Administrator (same product) | Soft Conflict — SHOULD NOT | Operational users SHOULD NOT administer the system in which they perform operational work. Exception requires documented business justification. |
| **SOD-04** | Elevated Operational User | Security Administrator (same product) | Soft Conflict — SHOULD NOT | Elevated operational users SHOULD NOT hold security administration authority for their own product. Exception requires documented approval from Security Architecture. |
page_texts.35:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#132-sod-enforcement]

### 13.2 SoD Enforcement

- Hard Conflict constraints (SHALL NOT) are mandatory. Products SHALL implement technical controls where feasible. Where technical enforcement is not achievable, the deviation SHALL follow the [standards exception request process](../../../governance/processes/standards-development.md#exception-request-process), and approved manual compensating controls SHALL be documented.

- Soft Conflict constraints (SHOULD NOT) require documented business justification and periodic review. Exceptions SHALL be reviewed at least annually.
- Products are responsible for detecting and remediating SoD violations identified during access reviews.
page_texts.36:
[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#133-sod-review-triggers]

### 13.3 SoD Review Triggers

Products SHALL conduct an SoD review when:
- A new Business Persona is created
- An existing persona is mapped to an additional archetype
- A user is assigned multiple roles in the same product
- An access review identifies a potential conflict

### 14.2 Adoption Requirements by Product Status

| Product Status | Adoption Requirement |
|----------------|----------------------|
| **New product (greenfield)** | SHALL adopt the enterprise archetype model and define Business Personas before implementing product roles. |
| **Active product undergoing role redesign** | SHALL align revised roles to enterprise archetypes before publishing the new role model. |
| **Active product with no planned role changes** | SHOULD complete archetype mapping within 12 months of this standard's effective date. |
| **Legacy product in maintenance-only mode** | MAY defer full adoption; SHALL complete archetype mapping as a minimum. |
| **DDI implementing a new state program** | SHALL use the product's published Business Personas as the starting point for state role definitions. |

[standards/security/authorization/STD-SEC-AUTHZ-002-enterprise-user-roles-architecture.md#143-minimum-viable-adoption-deliverables]

### 14.3 Minimum Viable Adoption Deliverables

Each product SHALL produce and maintain the following as evidence of adoption:

1. **Role-to-Archetype Mapping Register** — A table mapping each product role to its primary enterprise archetype. Format defined in Section 10.0.
2. **Business Persona Definitions** — A definition for each Tier 2 Business Persona following the format in Section 8.0.
3. **SoD Constraint Register** — A list of product-specific SoD constraints applicable to the product's roles, inclusive of the enterprise constraints in Section 13.1.
4. **Business Owner Designation** — A named business owner for each Business Persona.

### 14.4 Tooling and Implementation Notes

This standard does not prescribe any specific IAM, RBAC, or IGA tooling. Products SHALL implement the logical role model using whatever authorization mechanisms are available within the product's technology stack, consistent with the technical implementation guidance in [STD-SEC-AUTHZ-001](STD-SEC-AUTHZ-001-authorization-implementation.md).

### 15.4 State DDI Extension Example — Pharmacy, State of Fictive

A DDI implementing Pharmacy for a state program MAY further scope the `pharmacy:claims-processor` product role to reflect state-specific operational constraints.

| State Role | Extends | Restriction Applied | State Extension Register Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| `state-fictive:pharmacy:claims-processor-region-a` | `pharmacy:claims-processor` | Scoped to Region A claim types only | Required |
| `state-fictive:pharmacy:claims-processor-mco` | `pharmacy:claims-processor` | Scoped to MCO-submitted claims only | Required |

State extensions SHALL restrict scope. They SHALL NOT grant entitlements not present in the product role they extend.

## 17.0 Risks and Constraints

| Risk ID | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---------|------|------------|--------|------------|
| **R-01** | Products resist adopting the enterprise model, perceiving it as overhead | Medium | High | Communicate business value; minimize adoption burden; provide tooling and templates. |
| **R-02** | Enterprise archetypes are too coarse to map existing product roles accurately | Medium | Medium | Allow secondary archetype mappings for transitional periods; collect mapping feedback to inform archetype refinement. |
| **R-03** | DDI partners create state roles that expand rather than restrict product role scope | Medium | High | Require state extension registers; include GEURA compliance in DDI contractual obligations where feasible. |
| **R-04** | Adoption stalls due to resource constraints at the product level | High | Medium | Stage adoption requirements by product status; prioritize strategic products in Wave 1. |
| **R-05** | SoD conflicts identified during adoption are difficult to remediate due to legacy entitlement structures | Medium | High | Separate identification from remediation; document conflicts as a risk register item; remediate in subsequent product cycles. |
| **R-06** | Enterprise archetypes become stale and misaligned with evolving product landscapes | Low | High | Mandate annual review cadence; establish a change request process; assign EA ownership explicitly. |
| **R-07** | Products treat archetype mapping as a documentation exercise without real governance value | Medium | Medium | Integrate mapping register reviews into EA engagement checkpoints; require registers as part of architecture reviews. |

### Constraints

- This standard does not alter existing product authorization implementations. Products carry responsibility for their own entitlement models.
- No dedicated funding or staffing is assumed. Adoption relies on product teams absorbing mapping and governance activities within existing capacity.
- Contractual obligations between Gainwell and state programs take precedence over this standard where they conflict. Such conflicts SHALL be surfaced to Enterprise Architecture for resolution guidance.

## 18.0 Future Direction

The following capabilities represent logical extensions of this standard and are identified as future investment opportunities. They are NOT requirements of this standard.

| Future Capability | Description | Dependency on This Standard |
|---|---|---|
| **Enterprise Entitlement Catalog** | A machine-readable inventory of product entitlements mapped to enterprise roles, enabling automated access certification. | Requires role mapping registers from this standard as the structural foundation. |
| **IGA Platform Integration** | Adoption of an Identity Governance and Administration platform to automate provisioning, access reviews, and role certification. | Requires a clean enterprise role taxonomy (this standard) as the data model. |
| **Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)** | Extension of the role model to incorporate contextual attributes (e.g., state, program, organization) for dynamic authorization decisions. | Enterprise archetypes provide the role dimension that ABAC contextualizes. |
| **Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) / Externalized Authorization** | Separation of authorization logic from applications into a centralized policy engine. | Role archetypes inform policy subjects in externalized policy models. |
| **Zero Trust Access Model** | Continuous verification of identity, device posture, and context for every access request. | Enterprise role archetypes provide the identity claim structure that Zero Trust policies evaluate. |
| **Automated SoD Detection** | Real-time detection and alerting of SoD violations during provisioning. | Requires the SoD constraint register defined in this standard. |

The sequence of future capabilities is advisory. Actual investment sequencing is subject to Enterprise Architecture roadmap planning and business prioritization.

Use this template when documenting a new Business Persona as part of the governance process in Section 11.2. All fields are required unless marked optional.

status: 'proposed'              # proposed | under-review | approved | rejected | active | deprecated | retired
business_owner: ''              # Name and title of accountable business owner

|---|---|---|---|
